Kaavakuva, energia-akseli logaritmisessa: Diagram, an energy axis on a logarithmic scale: the photon energy in electronvolts from a tenth to ten million, each division ten times the previous one. Visible light is a narrow coloured band 1.7–3.3 electronvolts, and the photon of red LED light is 1.9 electronvolts. A dashed line at 12.6 electronvolts is the ionisation energy of a water molecule: to its left a photon does not ionise water, to its right it does. The photon of a dental X-ray, about 60 kiloelectronvolts, and the gamma photon of caesium-137, 662 kiloelectronvolts, are far to the right. Brackets below the axis: the differences between the energy levels of the electrons of an atom are of the order of electronvolts, those of the nucleus of kilo- and megaelectronvolts.
Kuvaaja mittakaavassa: jäljellä oleva os: Graph to scale: the remaining fraction as a function of the number n of half-lives or half-value thicknesses, n from zero to five. The curve starts at 1 and falls ever more gently. Dashed lines show that n = 1 gives a half, n = 2 a quarter and n = 3 an eighth. The curve approaches zero but does not reach it: decay and the attenuation of gamma radiation have no end point.

Tunnistuskaavio: mistä tunnistan, mitä l: Recognition chart: how do I tell which law to use? First see which quantity the task gives, then which sign fits. Frequency or wavelength of a photon: the photon energy is Planck's constant times the frequency. Light ejects electrons: in the photoelectric effect the photon energy is the work function plus the maximum kinetic energy of the electron. An atom emits or absorbs: a quantum jump, the photon energy is the difference between the upper and lower energy levels. A nucleus decays as time passes: the decay law, the amount left is the initial amount times e to the power minus the decay constant times the time. How many decays per second: the activity is the decay constant times the number of nuclei. Mass difference of a nuclear reaction: the released energy is the mass difference times the speed of light squared. The type of radiation matters: the equivalent dose is the radiation weighting factor times the absorbed dose. The distance from the source changes: for a point source the dose rate is inversely proportional to the square of the distance. Radiation passes through matter: the attenuation law, the intensity is the initial intensity times e to the power minus the attenuation coefficient times the thickness.
Kaavakuva, ei lukuarvoja. Vasemmalla pis: Schematic, no numerical values. On the left is a point source from which radiation leaves evenly in all directions. Around the source are two sphere surfaces, the nearer one at the distance r 1 and the farther one at the distance r 2. A beam of radiation from the source meets both surfaces. Farther away the same radiation is spread over a larger area. At the nearer surface the dose rate is H dot 1 and at the farther surface H dot 2.
